en: Toward the khan's city below,
Uncle Bakai, I have turned my crown's hair to wool.
For the sake of one orphan,
I have made my noble self a slave woman.
My dear hair, thick as a saddle-girth,
I comb toward my breast.
Since my lord went to the other world,
I look to another's favor.
Indeed, alas, treacherous world,
My forehead bone is sloping;
When my king died,
My means of living proved scant!
The hair at my nape is grass.
Since my hero died,
My ruin outweighs my delight
By a spear's length!
When the gray-maned hero died,
Was I to see a dark night?
Semetey, left by the gray-maned hero,
Carrying him, wandering to Bukhara—
Was such a day to come?
When my valiant one was alive,
I, the bereaved, unlucky one,
Was renowned at first.
Semetey, left as a gift,
I carried in flight toward Bukhara
At the age of thirty-two.
Uncle Bakai, consider:
Parted from my saint,
I wish to die of shame.
Uncle Bakai, my sultan,
I go on without dying,
Because this orphan, heir to a realm, exists.
Alas, I go on grieving in shame.
A soul does not die from grief;
I go on without dying, uncle,
Because this Semetey exists.
My dresses of every kind,
When I pull them, do not reach my neck.
Though I weep and lament until exhausted,
The lion gone to the other world
Has not drawn me into his embrace.
Uncle Bakai, a soul does not die of burning grief.
Rather than see this sorrow,
Uncle Bakai, why did I not die with my sultan?”
Weeping and crying out in earnest,
The mourning woman Kanykei
Stood sobbing and lamenting.
Her whole heart torn apart,
The widow left by the gray-maned hero
Shed tears from her eyes.
Kanykei wept in sorrow,
Unable to check her running nose.
The wretched soul grieved still more,
Unable to wipe away her tears.
The famed fierce woman Kanykei
Troubled her thoughts still more.
Kanykei held up to her face
The child left as a gift.
She stood sobbing, unable to die,
Unable to cut short her undying life,
And greatly troubled her thoughts.
Kanykei took as her support
The child left by her khan.
Kanykei, left by Manas,
Troubled her thoughts still more,
Lifting to her head
The child left by gray-maned Manas.
Then Bakai, the noble lion,
At Kanykei's sorrow
Could not stand for grief.
Showing that he was a khan,
That Koshoi, khan of the Katagan—
Taitoru he had given as a mourning gift
He had Kanykei mount.
With an easy ambling gait, gentle to ride,
Akborchuk, of good disposition,
For her to ride on the journey,
For her to attain her wish,
He had Chyiyrdy mount.
He gave a coat that kept out the heat.
Showing his lion's nature,
Precious yellow-patterned weft from Andijan,
Precious dark-patterned cloth from Bukhara,
A golden collar, copper sleeves,
Double mail with rings like larks' eyes,
A broad battle-coat with gold-thread trim,
That no musket-ball could pierce,
That no arrow could pass through,
Twelve silk garments and eight coats
He divided between the two to wear.
Khan Bakai acted as their father,
While Kanykei's heart burned.
He supplied their equipment and arms,
Showing that he was a khan.
An arrow-proof cloak of precious white cloth
He put upon Kanykei.
The gray belt that came from heaven
He fastened snugly about her waist.
Bakai wept bitterly in anguish,
The mighty one grieving for his orphan.
Then that noble khan Bakai
Gave them two winged steeds,
Gave them many skins of milk.
Weeping, Bakai pressed close,
And Semetey, still a babe in the cradle,
He entrusted to poor Kanykei.
“My spirited child, Kanykei,
You have set out for Bukhara.
Your road crosses hills and mountain passes.
May you encounter no enemy
And reach Bukhara safely.
My honored child, farewell!
My treasure, whom I counted on,
You have saddened wretched Bakai.
My precious Kanykei,
My saint left by my khan Manas,
When I look, you are my support,
King Manas, the fierce-maned wolf—
You were the support I held as his very self.
Oh, Kanykei, my foal,
You were a lion among women.
While my great Manas lived,
You were a city of wisdom.
Parted from the great ones,
Now that I have grown old,
I was the one to be trampled down.
Instead of dying crushed,
I, this old man Bakai,
Shall grieve for twelve years.
‘Kanykei, left after the ruin—
What news has come of her?’
I shall go on praying.
I shall seek news through those who tell it;
In my sorrow, I, Bakai,
Shall question those who come.
If I hear good news of you,
I shall make an offering to Baabedin.
If I hear bad news of you,
I shall cut short my wretched life.
You are a woman, Kanykei,
Yet I shall know you are a hero.
I shall tend the camels without tiring
And ride the gray winged steed.
At Bek-Jailoo, above Besh-Tash,
I, Bakai, shall camp in hiding.
My treasure of gold coins
I shall spend in its entirety.
From the one Creator, Allah,
I shall beg for Semetey.
If my orphan returns safely,
Khan Bakai will have lived to see his day.
After twelve years, Semetey—
If my little one is delayed,
Your dignified elder Bakai
Will die if he never comes.
God has torn my thoughts apart.
Bring him here, Kanykei,
Let me breathe his scent as a keepsake—
The child left by the warrior.”
When Kanykei heard this,
Her heart was deeply grieved.
Kanykei handed him
The child left by the warrior Manas.
Khan Bakai took into his arms
His dark-blazed young hawk.
He clasped him to his breast and sobbed,
His little one left by Manas.
His soft, gray-speckled falcon
He hugged close to his breast,
His gray goshawk, his morning star.
Then old Bakai's
Thoughts were grievously torn apart.
As though they were about to part forever,
Tears streamed from his eyes.
While Bakai stood thus,
Kanykei and Chyiyrdy,
Those two mourners, wept bitterly.
Breathing the scent of the child's cheek,
The renowned Khan Bakai wept:
“My hoof left by the winged steed!”
Unable to stand, Bakai wailed.
“My lamp left by the falcon,
My pennant fastened to a spear,
You have gone far from my side,
My gift left by the generous one,
My spring flowing down the valley,
From peerless, precious Manas,
My little one, whom I saw after his death.
My orphan, fleeing to Bukhara,
Have you eaten your allotted salt?
Did you mean your grieving elder Bakai
To die choking on sorrow like this?
Traveling far on a six-month road,
Are you the one who must waste away?
Unable to die of wounded pride,
Am I the one who must suffer?
Did you mean all that treasury's gold
To be scattered, my orphan?
His eyes reddened like a raven's,
His white beard hanging down,
Did you mean your aged elder Bakai
To bear such suffering for you?
To the city of Temir Khan,
Were you the orphan who must wander?
And I, helpless in the steppe,
Was I to be the Bakai who howled?
Fighting with spears, breaking the ranks,
In the city of Beijing with its khakans,
Why did I not die there?
Rather than weep with grief in the steppe
And witness this calamity,
Beside the leopard Manas, the fierce wolf,
Why did I not die there?
Alas, Manas, if only you had not died!
Kanykei suffers humiliation,
And Semetey goes away with her.
I am utterly bereft of support,
Chyiyrdy, whom I counted on—
I am parted from my mother.
Without dying or perishing, I, Bakai—
Have I camped along the valley?
Parted from those who sustained me,
Now that I have grown old,
Have I become like an extinguished fire?
O God, hiding my caravan-sized frame,
Weeping in sorrow, I, Bakai—
Was this a day for bearing grief?
You who drove the caravans to flight,
My falcon Manas, if only you had not passed away!
Wandering without kin to Bukhara,
Semetey, whom I saw after his father's death,
Oh, do not forget me and wander away!
Seen today, gone tomorrow,
The deceiver that keeps deluding us—
Such is this dung of a world!
What Allah lays upon our heads,
We have no choice but to bear.
You have set out for Bukhara,
Oh, Kanykei, my foal.
Let me tell you the landmarks:
The famed sacred capital of sheikhs,
And the chief cities, Kokand and Andijan.
Let me describe the people,
Oh, Kanykei, my foal.
If you travel onward from here,
Covering ground without sparing your horse,
You will come to rolling hills,
To a ridge crossed by hilly passes.
Its valley is hilly, broad and flat;
A single road follows the ridge.
That is the pass amid the hills.
Oh, Kanykei, my foal,
That road is called Aman-Jol;
It is the road to Bukhara.
Its corners loom dimly,
